summary: Limestone tower of 1859 on Chantry Island off Southampton, Lake Huron: one of the Imperial Towers, automated in 1954, its keeper's house restored by volunteers; boat tours only.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1857 (Wikidata) is the date of a temporary fixed light shown from the unfinished tower. The permanent light, with its lantern room and second-order lens, was first shown at the opening of navigation in 1859 (LighthouseFriends). The story gives both dates.

The Coast Guard list (current official list) gives 28.0 m for the structure above ground and 29.5 m for the focal height, which the record keeps. LighthouseFriends gives 26.2 m for the tower and 31.4 m for the focal height. The story reports the disagreement; the Wikipedia article's 26 m and 31 m are a lead only and are not cited.
LighthouseFriends gives 'roughly one kilometre offshore' in its introduction and 'roughly 1.5 km (1 mile) offshore' in its map section. The story gives the range, 1 to 1.5 km.

notes_for_editor: (1) Sources: the keeper roster, the rescues and most dates come from LighthouseFriends (a secondary compilation that quotes the Commissioners' reports and the Department of Marine). The rescue accounts (1879, 1892, 1906) are LighthouseFriends' only; Chronicling America searches for Chantry Island, the Nettie Woodward and the Mary and Lucy found nothing usable. Not checked against Canadian newspapers (not in our corpus). (2) The 1852-53 and 1855-56 Commissioners' quotations are as LighthouseFriends prints them; the primary reports are not in the corpus. (3) The 1900 keepers' list (p. 122) is OCR'd and the names and stations sit in separate columns: the match of 'Lambert, Wm. McGregor' to 1 October 1880 is by position, and the story gives the date only against the station. The LighthouseFriends roster is the basis for the William Lambert line. (4) The 1917 table: the keeper's name is garbled in the OCR ('K'.ippert'); the Klippert identity comes from LighthouseFriends, matched by the station line only. (5) Dates in the Canadian annual reports: the fiscal years end 30 June up to 1903 and 31 March after; cited as the year each report covers. (6) The currency sign on the 1855 breakwater appropriation is garbled in the cached LighthouseFriends text, so no amount is given. (7) The Mary and Lucy keeper's son: LighthouseFriends calls Duncan Ross Lambert the eighth of eleven children; the story says 'the keeper's son' only. (8) The Canadian Register cites a Federal Heritage Buildings Review Office report, 'Four Imperial Towers' (no. 90-213), where LighthouseFriends counts six Imperial Towers; not reconciled. (9) The Marine Heritage Society (1997) and LighthouseFriends (1998) give different founding years. (10) Wikipedia was read for leads only (its Lighthouse height and lens figures) and is not cited. (11) Parks Canada's federal heritage page for CRHP's federal designation (FHBRO 4463) did not load; the 1991 heritage date in the record is not confirmed here. (12) The current light: the Coast Guard list (read 27 Oct 2026) gives 'Seasonal (in place year round)'; the access and tour facts are from the Marine Heritage Society page and LighthouseFriends, both undated, and should be checked before the public season. (13) Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1900 keepers' row (p. 122, scan p. 219) was checked on the page image: 'Lambert, Wm. McGregor' sits on the same line as Chantry Island and 1 October 1880, so the name and date are matched by row, not by column position alone. (14) The 1906 Cavalier of Sarnia wreck happened in the night of 31 August to 1 September (LighthouseFriends: 'During the previous night'); the rescue was on the morning of 1 September. (15) Quotations that LighthouseFriends gives second-hand (the 1852-53 Commissioners, the 1855-56 breakwater report, the 1876 inspector, the Fo'c'sle interview) are attributed to it in the story. (16) The distance offshore is given as a range because LighthouseFriends gives two figures. (17) Several LighthouseFriends sentences were reworded to our own words; the story keeps one short quotation from it at most.
